title: Ozone depletion

definition.text: Ozone depletion is a lowered total amount of ozone in the upper stratosphere plus a much larger springtime decrease over the polar regions, observed since the late 1970s.

facts.text: The main causes are manufactured halocarbons used as refrigerants, solvents, propellants and foam-blowing agents (CFCs, HCFCs, halons), called ozone-depleting substances.
The ozone layer absorbs UVB light, so depletion raises surface UVB, which could increase skin cancer; this was the reason for the Montreal Protocol.

Since the Montreal Protocol was adopted and strengthened, concentrations of the most significant CFCs have declined; effective equivalent chlorine peaked in 1994 and had dropped about 10 percent by 2008.
The Vienna and Montreal conventions were put in place before a scientific consensus existed or key uncertainties were resolved.
Frank Sherwood Rowland and Mario Molina suggested in 1974 that long-lived organic halogen compounds such as CFCs could deplete ozone.

related: Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer

title: Antarctic ozone hole
article: Ozone depletion#Ozone hole and its causes

definition.text: The Antarctic ozone hole is an area of the Antarctic stratosphere where ozone has dropped to as low as 33 percent of pre-1975 values.

facts.text: It occurs in the Antarctic spring, September to early December, when strong westerly winds form a polar vortex in which over 50 percent of lower stratospheric ozone is destroyed.
British Antarctic Survey scientists reported it in Nature in May 1985; the decline was far larger than anticipated.
It is measured as reduced total column ozone in Dobson units; actual hole values are in the 150-100 DU range.

title: Ozone-depleting substances
article: Ozone depletion#Observations on ozone layer depletion > Compounds in the atmosphere > CFCs and related compounds

definition.text: Ozone-depleting substances are halogenated chemicals, chiefly CFCs, that are mainly responsible for man-made ozone depletion.

facts.text: The total effective chlorine and bromine in the stratosphere is expressed as equivalent effective stratospheric chlorine (EESC).
Very short-lived substances, which degrade in under 6 months, are allowed by the Montreal Protocol; 90% are natural, 10% manmade such as dichloromethane.
CFCs are well mixed globally and are not kept from the stratosphere by their weight, since wind mixes atmospheric gases.

definition.text: The Global Environment Facility is a multilateral environmental fund giving grants and blended finance to developing countries for biodiversity, climate change, international waters, land degradation, pollutants and forests.

facts.text: It is the largest multilateral funder of biodiversity, distributing over $1 billion a year on average; it has provided more than $22 billion in grants and mobilized $120 billion in co-financing for over 5,200 projects.
It began in October 1991 as a $1 billion World Bank pilot and became a permanent separate institution at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit; the World Bank has been trustee since 1994.
It is the financial mechanism for the CBD, UNFCCC, UNCCD, Stockholm Convention and Minamata Convention, and supports the Montreal Protocol.
Donors pledged a record $5.33 billion in June 2022 for the replenishment cycle running to June 2026.
Its Small Grants Programme supported nearly 27,000 civil society and community initiatives in 136 countries.

definition.text: The GEF funds the incremental or additional costs of turning a project with national benefits into one with global environmental benefits.

facts.text: The GEF provides new and additional grants and concessional funding to cover those incremental costs.

definition.text: The GEF is governed through an Assembly, a Council, a Secretariat, agencies, a scientific panel and an Independent Evaluation Office.

facts.text: The Assembly of all 184 member countries meets every three to four years at ministerial level.
The Council, the main governing body, has 32 members (14 developed, 16 developing, 2 transition economies), meets twice annually and decides by consensus.
The Independent Evaluation Office reports directly to the Council and evaluates GEF impact and effectiveness.
